questions.q: What is the first question that determines a model's parallelism strategy, according to this lesson's decision framework?
options: How many quiz questions the course includes
Whether the model's weights, activations, and optimizer state fit on a single GPU
Whether the dataset is larger than 1 terabyte
Whether the model was trained with LoRA or full fine-tuning
questions.explain: Whether the model fits on one GPU is the fork in the road: if it does, data parallelism (with ZeRO 1/2 as needed) suffices; if not, sharding or explicit model parallelism becomes necessary.

questions.q: When a model doesn't fit on a single GPU but training stays on one multi-GPU node, what is the recommended next-cheapest lever before reaching for tensor or pipeline parallelism?
options: Immediately switch to 3D parallelism across many nodes
ZeRO stage 3 or FSDP's FULL_SHARD combined with activation checkpointing, since both are simple config flags or wrapping calls
Reduce the model's parameter count by removing layers
Switch the optimizer to plain SGD
questions.explain: ZeRO-3/FSDP plus activation checkpointing is comparatively simple to enable and doesn't require restructuring the model's code, making it the path of least complexity before adding explicit model parallelism.

questions.q: Why does tensor parallelism typically stay confined within a single server rather than stretching across nodes?
options: Because tensor parallelism doesn't require any communication at all
Because its frequent in-layer all-reduces need the low latency of a fast interconnect like NVLink, which is available within a server but not typically between servers
Because tensor parallelism only works with pipeline parallelism, never alone
Because tensor parallelism is incompatible with data parallelism
questions.explain: Tensor parallelism requires communication inside every layer's forward and backward pass, many times per step, which needs the low latency and high bandwidth of an intra-server interconnect like NVLink to stay efficient.

options: Combining data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism simultaneously, each operating on its own axis of the cluster
Using three different learning rates during training
questions.explain: 3D parallelism combines all three parallelism axes at once: tensor parallel within a server, pipeline parallel across servers, and data parallel replicating the whole tensor+pipeline structure, as frameworks like Megatron-DeepSpeed orchestrate.

questions.q: In a 3D parallelism setup with tensor-parallel size 8, pipeline-parallel size 4, and data-parallel size 16, how many total GPUs does the configuration use?
questions.explain: The three parallelism degrees multiply together to determine total GPU usage: 8 × 4 × 16 = 512 GPUs, each playing a specific role across the three axes.
